topics.title: From geocentric skies to Kepler's law of orbits

learn.hook: The same force that makes a mango drop from a tree in Malihabad keeps the Moon circling the Earth. It took humanity two thousand years to see that.
points: Everything near the Earth tends to fall towards it. The motion of planets puzzled thinkers for centuries: Ptolemy's geocentric model put the Earth at the centre.
Aryabhata (5th century CE) described the Earth rotating on its axis; Copernicus (16th century) proposed the heliocentric model with the Sun at the centre.

Tycho Brahe made precise naked-eye records of planetary positions; Kepler analysed them to find three laws; Galileo showed all bodies fall with the same acceleration; Newton explained it all with universal gravitation.
Kepler's first law (law of orbits): every planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus.
Perihelion: the point of closest approach to the Sun; aphelion: the farthest point.

example.q: A planet's orbit has perihelion distance 1.0 AU and aphelion distance 1.5 AU. Find the semi-major axis.
steps: The major axis = perihelion + aphelion distance = 2.5 AU.

learn.reallife: Jantar Mantar observatories built in Jaipur and Delhi were used to track the Sun, Moon and planets with remarkable precision long before telescopes were common in India.

topics.title: Kepler's laws of areas and periods

learn.hook: The Earth moves fastest in early January, when it is closest to the Sun. Kepler's second law predicted this centuries ago.
points: Second law (law of areas): the line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time.
Reason: gravity is a central force, so it exerts no torque about the Sun and the planet's angular momentum L is conserved. Areal velocity dA/dt = L/(2m) = constant.
Hence a planet moves faster near perihelion and slower near aphelion: v_p r_p = v_a r_a.
Third law (law of periods): T² ∝ a³, where a is the semi-major axis. T²/a³ is nearly the same for all planets of the Sun.

example.q: A comet's speed at perihelion (r = 1 AU) is 60 km s⁻¹. Find its speed at aphelion (r = 5 AU).
steps: Angular momentum is conserved: v_p r_p = v_a r_a.

learn.reallife: ISRO's Mars Orbiter Mission moved in a highly elliptical orbit around Mars, speeding up near periapsis exactly as the law of areas predicts.

teach.ask: Gappu thinks all planets move at the same steady speed. Explain Kepler's second and third laws and why the second law holds.
teach.praise: Closer to the Sun means faster, because angular momentum is conserved. And T² ∝ a³ ties all planets together!
teach.nudge: Where does a planet move fastest? Which conserved quantity explains it? How are period and distance linked?

learn.hook: You and the person next to you attract each other gravitationally right now. The force is about a millionth of a newton, far too tiny to feel.
points: Every particle attracts every other particle with F = Gm₁m₂/r², along the line joining them.
Vector form: the force on m₂ due to m₁ is F₂₁ = −(Gm₁m₂/r²) r̂₁₂, where r̂₁₂ points from m₁ to m₂; the minus sign shows attraction.
Gravitational force is always attractive, central (along the line of centres) and obeys superposition: the net force is the vector sum of forces from each mass.
Three equal masses at the vertices of an equilateral triangle exert zero net force on a mass at the centroid (by symmetry).

example.q: Find the gravitational force between two 100 kg spheres whose centres are 1 m apart (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
steps: Tiny compared with their weights (about 980 N each).

learn.reallife: The tides at the Gulf of Khambhat, among the highest in India, are driven by the Moon's and Sun's gravitational pull on the oceans.

topics.title: Shell theorem, Newton's Moon test and measuring G

learn.hook: Newton asked: if gravity reaches the apple, does it reach the Moon? He checked using nothing more than the Moon's orbit and the inverse-square law.
points: Shell theorem: a uniform spherical shell attracts an outside point mass as if all its mass were at its centre. Inside the shell, the net force is zero.
Moon test: the Moon is about 60 Earth radii away. Its centripetal acceleration a_m = 4π²R_m/T² ≈ 0.0027 m s⁻², and g/a_m ≈ 3600 = 60², just as the inverse-square law predicts.
Cavendish (1798) measured G with a torsion balance: two small lead spheres on a rod hung from a fine wire, attracted by two large spheres; the twist of the wire gave the force.
Accepted value: G ≈ 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².

example.q: Show that the Moon's acceleration agrees with the inverse-square law if the Moon is 60 Earth radii away.
steps: At the surface (r = R), acceleration = g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻².
At r = 60R, acceleration should be g/60² = 9.8/3600.
= 0.0027 m s⁻², matching 4π²R_m/T² for the Moon.

learn.reallife: Precise measurements of G are still being improved worldwide, because G is the least precisely known of the fundamental constants.

topics.title: Acceleration due to gravity at the Earth's surface

learn.hook: Knowing just g, the Earth's radius and G, you can 'weigh' the entire Earth from your physics lab.
points: Treat the Earth as concentric uniform shells: for any outside point, the Earth acts as a point mass M_E at its centre.
At the surface: mg = GM_E m/R_E², so g = GM_E/R_E².
Mass of the Earth: M_E = gR_E²/G = 9.8 × (6.37 × 10⁶)²/(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹) ≈ 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg.
Weight W = mg. g does not depend on the mass of the falling body, so (without air) all bodies fall with the same acceleration.

example.q: A planet has twice the Earth's mass and twice its radius. Compare g on it with g on the Earth.
steps: So g on the planet is g/2.

learn.reallife: Gaganyaan astronauts training in Bengaluru learn that their mass stays the same in orbit, while the weight they feel changes with g and with acceleration.

topics.title: Variation of g with height and depth

learn.hook: Climbers on Mount Everest weigh about 0.3% less than at sea level, and in a deep mine g also drops. The surface is where g peaks.
points: Height h: g(h) = GM/(R + h)² = g(1 + h/R)⁻² ≈ g(1 − 2h/R) for h ≪ R.
Depth d: only the inner sphere of radius (R − d) attracts (the outer shell gives zero), so g(d) = g(1 − d/R).
g is maximum at the surface, decreases with height and with depth, and is zero at the centre.
At h = R, g becomes g/4; at d = R/2, g becomes g/2. Small heights: g falls by about twice as fast with height as with depth.

example.q: A body weighs 72 N on the surface. Find its weight at height R/2 and at depth R/2.

learn.reallife: Geologists of the Geological Survey of India use tiny variations of g (gravity surveys) to locate dense ore bodies and oil-bearing rocks underground.

learn.hook: Lifting a satellite to orbit costs energy. How much? You can't use mgh for thousands of kilometres; you need the general formula.
points: Gravitational force is conservative, so we can define potential energy: the work done by gravity depends only on start and end positions.
Near the surface (h ≪ R): the PE difference between heights h₁ and h₂ is mg(h₂ − h₁).
General expression, taking PE = 0 at infinity: W(r) = −GM_E m/r for r ≥ R_E. It is negative and increases (towards zero) as r increases.
Work needed to move m from r₁ to r₂ = W(r₂) − W(r₁) = GM_E m(1/r₁ − 1/r₂).

example.q: Find the work needed to raise a 1 kg mass from the Earth's surface to a height R (in terms of GM/R).
steps: = GMm/2R = ½ gR m (using GM = gR²).

learn.reallife: PSLV launches to sun-synchronous orbits at about 700 km lift satellites high enough that mgh is no longer accurate: engineers use −GMm/r.

topics.title: Gravitational potential and systems of particles

learn.hook: The total gravitational energy of a star cluster is the sum of the energy of every pair. Four particles? That's six pairs.
points: Gravitational potential V at a point = PE per unit mass: V = −GM/r (unit J kg⁻¹). It is a scalar.
Potentials from several masses add as scalars: V = −G Σ mᵢ/rᵢ.
PE of a system of particles = sum over all pairs: U = −G Σ mᵢmⱼ/rᵢⱼ (each pair counted once).
Four equal masses m at the corners of a square of side l: 4 sides and 2 diagonals (l√2), so U = −(Gm²/l)(4 + √2). Potential at the centre (distance l/√2 from each) = −4√2 Gm/l.

example.q: Three equal masses m are at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side a. Find the PE of the system.
steps: Number of pairs = 3, each separated by a.

learn.reallife: Astrophysicists at TIFR estimate whether a gas cloud will collapse into stars by comparing its total gravitational PE with its thermal energy.

Square of side l: number of side pairs

learn.hook: Throw a ball up at 11.2 km s⁻¹ (ignoring air) and it never comes back. That's the Earth's escape speed.
points: A body escapes if its total energy is ≥ 0: ½mv² − GMm/R ≥ 0.
Minimum (escape) speed: v_e = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR). For the Earth (g = 9.8 m s⁻², R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m) v_e ≈ 11.2 km s⁻¹.
Escape speed does not depend on the mass of the body or the direction of launch (ignoring air).
The Moon's escape speed is only about 2.3 km s⁻¹. It is so low that the faster gas molecules escape over time, so the Moon has no atmosphere.
Between two fixed spheres: a projectile must reach the 'neutral point' where the two pulls balance; beyond it, the far sphere pulls it in.

example.q: Calculate the Earth's escape speed with g = 9.8 m s⁻² and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m.

learn.reallife: Chandrayaan missions do not leave Earth at 11.2 km s⁻¹ directly; they raise their orbit step by step with engine burns, gaining energy gradually.

teach.ask: Gappu thinks a heavier rocket needs a higher escape speed. Explain escape speed using energy conservation.
teach.praise: Kinetic energy must beat GMm/R, and since m cancels, every object needs the same 11.2 km/s!
teach.nudge: What condition on energy lets a body escape? Does its mass matter?

topics.title: Earth satellites: orbital speed and period

learn.hook: A satellite skimming just above the Earth would circle the planet in about 85 minutes, faster than a cricket Test session!
points: Satellites are natural (the Moon) or artificial (INSAT, Cartosat). In a circular orbit, gravity provides the centripetal force: mv²/(R + h) = GMm/(R + h)².
Orbital speed v = √(GM/(R + h)); it decreases with height. Near the surface v ≈ √(gR) ≈ 7.9 km s⁻¹.
Period T = 2π√((R + h)³/GM), so T² ∝ (R + h)³: Kepler's third law for satellites.
For h ≪ R: T ≈ 2π√(R/g) ≈ 85 minutes.
From a moon's orbit we can find the planet's mass: M = 4π²r³/(GT²) (e.g. Mars from its moon Phobos; Earth from the Moon).

example.q: Find the period of a satellite orbiting just above the Earth's surface (R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, g = 9.8 m s⁻²).

learn.reallife: ISRO's geostationary communication satellites like GSAT orbit at about 36000 km height with a 24-hour period, staying fixed over India.

quiz.q: Which of these is a natural satellite of the Earth?
quiz.explain: The Moon is the Earth's only natural satellite. Cartosat, INSAT and the ISS are artificial satellites placed in orbit by humans.
quiz.mistake: Confuses natural satellites with man-made ones

teach.ask: Gappu wonders why the ISS whizzes around in about 90 minutes while the Moon takes a month. Explain orbital speed and period.
teach.praise: Gravity is the centripetal force. Farther out, the speed drops and the period grows as r^(3/2)!
teach.nudge: What force keeps a satellite in orbit? How do speed and period change with distance?

learn.hook: To move a satellite to a higher orbit, you must ADD energy, even though it will end up moving more slowly. Strange but true.
points: Kinetic energy in a circular orbit of radius r = R + h: K = GMm/(2r).
Potential energy: U = −GMm/r.
Total energy E = K + U = −GMm/(2r). It is negative for a bound orbit, and K = −E, U = 2E.
Energy to move from orbit r₁ to r₂: ΔE = (GMm/2)(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) > 0 for r₂ > r₁.
Conceptual points: gravity cannot be shielded by any material; weight changes with height and depth; g is slightly smaller at the equator than at the poles (Earth's rotation and bulge).

example.q: A satellite in an orbit of radius 2R has total energy E. What is its energy in an orbit of radius 4R, and how much energy is needed to shift it?

learn.reallife: Satellite operators at ISRO's ISTRAC in Bengaluru fire thrusters to raise orbits that slowly decay because of thin atmospheric drag.
